figure: Figure 11.1 — Discrete vs continuous batching (Orca-style slot diagram)
issue: The caption assigns the time dimension to two mutually exclusive encodings. It states both 'The horizontal axis is time (decode steps / iterations)' and 'each row is one decode step'. Both cannot hold: if rows are decode steps, the horizontal axis must be batch slots, not time; if the horizontal axis is time, rows must be batch slots/sequences. The drawing settles it against the row clause — the bottom axis carries a rightward arrow labelled 'time (decode steps / iterations)', the figure calls itself an 'Orca-style slot diagram', the in-figure note says 'every shown request is in the per-token decode phase' (requests are the drawn objects), and the caption's own next clause — 'the step boundaries are staggered across rows as the scheduler admits new requests and evicts finished ones' — is only meaningful if rows are slots admitted at different times (a sequence admitted at time t has its step-1 boundary offset from one admitted at t=0). Therefore the clause 'each row is one decode step' is affirmatively wrong; it should read 'each row is one batch slot' (equivalently, 'each column is one decode step'). As printed, the caption misstates the diagram's encoding for the chapter's core concept.
evidence: Quoted caption, PDF 200 / printed 180: 'The horizontal axis is time (decode steps / iterations); each row is one decode step, and in the continuous panel the step boundaries are staggered across rows as the scheduler admits new requests and evicts finished ones.' In-figure axis label: 'time (decode steps / iterations)' with a rightward arrow. In-figure note: 'Decode-only illustration: every shown request is in the per-token decode phase.' In-figure label: 'new sequences (green) snap into freed slots.'
acceptance_test: The caption assigns exactly one axis to time and the other to slots/sequences, and the assignment matches the drawn axis arrow and the 'Orca-style slot diagram' description — e.g., 'The horizontal axis is time (decode steps / iterations); each row is one batch slot, and in the continuous panel the step boundaries are staggered across rows as the scheduler admits new requests and evicts finished ones.' Re-read: no clause places time on both axes.

issue: Under the only self-consistent reading (rows = batch slots, horizontal = time), the four discrete-panel rows appear at 150 dpi to carry in-flight (blue) segments of identical length ending at the same x, followed by identical idle (pink) segments. If that is what is drawn, the panel is internally contradictory: (a) no sequence finishes 'early' relative to another, so the in-figure label 'GPU slots idle (pink) when a sequence finishes early' has no visible cause; (b) no row extends to the right edge, so there is no 'slowest member' holding the batch open, yet the pink region and the 'next batch waits' box both assert the batch continues past x of the blue segments; (c) the caption's causal claim — 'a batch is locked until its slowest member finishes, so short outputs idle in the trailing slots' — is not exhibited by the geometry. The entire pedagogical point of the panel is that output-length variance creates the bubble; the drawing must show variance. Note the continuous panel on the same figure does vary its rows, so the capability existed. Confidence is medium because this is judged from a 150 dpi render; escalate to P1 if confirmed at print resolution.
evidence: Rendered page PDF 200 / printed 180: discrete panel rows 1-4 each show [blue block][pink block] with the blue blocks terminating at the same horizontal position; no row's blue segment extends beyond the others. Quoted in-figure label: 'GPU slots idle (pink) when a sequence finishes early'. Quoted caption: 'a batch is locked until its slowest member finishes, so short outputs idle in the trailing slots'. Quoted legend: 'idle slot (bubble)' / 'sequence in flight'.
acceptance_test: At print resolution, the discrete panel shows at least one row whose blue (sequence in flight) segment extends visibly beyond the others — the slowest sequence — while shorter rows turn pink at earlier x positions, so the trailing pink region is visibly caused by early finishers and the batch's end is visibly set by the longest row. Alternatively, if the drawn geometry is intentional, the in-figure label and caption are rewritten to describe what is actually drawn.

figure: Figure 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links (and Note 11.3-1 on the facing page)
issue: Two locations in the same argument give different token counts for the same ~35 GB per-request KV payload, and one of the stated multiplications does not reproduce its own result. Note 11.3-1 derives the payload as '13,000 tokens × 2.62 MB/token'; Figure 11.3 labels the same payload 'illustrative 13.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'. Recomputation: 13,000 × 2.62 MB = 34,060 MB = 34.06 GB, which does not round to ~35 GB under ordinary rounding (it rounds to 34 GB); 13,300 × 2.62 MB = 34,846 MB = 34.85 GB ≈ 35 GB. So the figure's token count reproduces the printed ~35 GB and the Note's does not, while the Note presents its multiplication as the derivation of that number. This is a load-bearing number: ~35 GB drives the transfer times (0.08 s / 0.9 s) and the aggregate caveat (35 GB × 40 req/s = 1.4 TB/s), both of which are otherwise internally correct. The defect is the derivation and the cross-location disagreement, not the downstream arithmetic.
evidence: Note 11.3-1, PDF 204 / printed 184: 'The ~35 GB is 13,000 tokens × 2.62 MB/token (§9.8).' Figure 11.3 panel headers, PDF 205 / printed 185: 'illustrative 13.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA' above '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node)' and '~35 GB ≈ 0.9 s (cross-host)'. Recomputed: 13,000 × 2.62 = 34.06 GB; 13,300 × 2.62 = 34.85 GB. Downstream checks that pass: 35 ÷ 450 = 0.0778 ≈ 0.08 s; 35 ÷ 40 = 0.875 ≈ 0.9 s; 35 × 40 = 1,400 GB/s = 1.4 TB/s.
acceptance_test: Note 11.3-1, Figure 11.3 (both panel headers), and §9.8 if it states a context length all carry the same token count, and the printed multiplication reproduces the printed ~35 GB within the printed precision — e.g., everywhere '13,300 tokens × 2.62 MB/token = 34.8 GB ≈ 35 GB'. A grep for '13,000' and '13.3K' in this argument returns one value.

issue: The caption says 'The panels show the canonical configuration (TP all-reduce per layer; PP with a small fixed microbatch count)' while the panels draw tensor parallel across 2 GPUs and pipeline parallel across 3. The book's canonical answer, stated on printed 174, is intra-host TP=8 ('the book's ~70B/8×H100 baseline uses intra-host TP=8'). The parenthetical defines only the collective and the microbatch count as canonical, but the word 'configuration' also covers device counts, so a careful reader can infer that TP=2 / PP=3 is the canonical setup — a false inference from a technically correct label. This is exactly the class of inference a schematic figure should not permit.
evidence: Quoted caption, PDF 187 / printed 167: 'The panels show the canonical configuration (TP all-reduce per layer; PP with a small fixed microbatch count); substitute the actual collective and schedule for the target stack.' Panel A draws 'GPU 0' / 'GPU 1' with W₀ / W₁; Panel B draws 'GPU 0 layers 1-8 / GPU 1 layers 9-16 / GPU 2 layers 17-24'. Contrasting prose, PDF 194 / printed 174: 'the book's ~70B/8×H100 baseline uses intra-host TP=8'.
acceptance_test: The caption narrows the scope of 'canonical', e.g., 'The panels show the canonical communication pattern (TP all-reduce per layer; PP with a small fixed microbatch count); device counts and layer counts are schematic — substitute the actual collective, rank count, and schedule for the target stack.' No reader can take the drawn 2-GPU TP or 3-stage PP as the book's baseline.

issue: Panel C asserts 'throughput scales linearly' as an unqualified consequence of 'independent replicas, no sync'. Linear scaling is the idealization, not a property of the pattern in deployment: it degrades under output-length load imbalance (the slowest replica sets batch completion wherever any global barrier exists), shared router/load-balancer or prefix-cache bottlenecks, network or storage limits on the data path, and per-replica memory ceilings that cap admitted concurrency. The figure carries [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual] in the caption, but that label binds the caption span, not this drawn clause, and the sentence is phrased as a law. Counterexample at the regime boundary: 8 replicas behind one router whose egress is saturated — aggregate throughput stops scaling at the router, with no change to the replicas.
evidence: Quoted panel C text, PDF 187 / printed 167: 'inference: independent replicas, no sync · throughput scales linearly'. Quoted caption tail: '[ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'.
acceptance_test: The panel reads 'throughput scales linearly with replica count (idealized: shared routing, load imbalance, and per-replica memory caps subtract)' or an equivalent qualifier, so the claim's scope matches its evidence.

figure: Figure 11.2 — Serving = four orthogonal concerns (box label + caption) vs Figure 11.3 caption
issue: Mixed -isation/-ization spelling for the same concept across two adjacent figures. Figure 11.2's box reads 'RESOURCE SPECIALISATION' and its caption repeats 'resource specialisation = P/D disaggregation' and 'resource specialisation joins when the workload outgrows a node'; the Figure 11.3 caption on the next page reads 'the specialization benefit exceeds that transfer plus routing overhead'. One is a visible figure label, so the inconsistency is not buried in prose.
evidence: PDF 204 / printed 184, Figure 11.2 fourth box: 'RESOURCE SPECIALISATION'; caption: 'resource specialisation = P/D disaggregation (separate prefill and decode pools)'. PDF 205 / printed 185, Figure 11.3 caption: 'disaggregation pays only when the specialization benefit exceeds that transfer plus routing overhead.'
acceptance_test: A case-insensitive search for 'speciali' across the manuscript returns exactly one spelling form; the Figure 11.2 box label and both captions agree.

issue: The two link rates are drawn with equal visual authority but are different evidence classes. '450 GB/s' is a first-party H100/NVLink per-direction specification (and Note 11.3-1 on printed 184 correctly scopes it: 'at NVLink's 450 GB/s per direction'). '40 GB/s' is an assumed or example fabric rate: nothing on the page names a fabric, gives a source, or marks it as an assumption, yet it is the number that produces the panel's headline '~35 GB ≈ 0.9 s (cross-host)' and therefore the figure's central 'transfer cost is the term that decides whether P/D disaggregation pays' conclusion. The caption's [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] labels bind the caption span, not the drawn glyph. A reader can reasonably take 40 GB/s as a stated property of 'the fabric' in general. (If §9 or an earlier chapter defines 40 GB/s as the canonical fabric assumption, the fix is a cross-reference rather than a relabel — that location was NOT VERIFIED in this pass.)
evidence: PDF 205 / printed 185, panel B header: '~35 GB ≈ 0.9 s (cross-host)'; panel B KV arrow label: '40 GB/s'; panel A KV arrow label: '450 GB/s'; caption tail: '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'. PDF 204 / printed 184, Note 11.3-1: '(B) cross-host, over the fabric: at 40 GB/s the same transfer 35 ÷ 40 ≈ 0.9 s'. Recomputed: 35 ÷ 40 = 0.875 ≈ 0.9 s (arithmetic correct; the issue is the evidence class of the 40, not the division).
acceptance_test: Panel B labels the rate as an assumption or example — e.g., '40 GB/s (assumed fabric)' — or the Figure 11.3 caption explicitly scopes it ('link rates: 450 GB/s is the H100 NVLink per-direction specification; 40 GB/s is an assumed cross-host fabric rate'), or a cross-reference points to where the 40 GB/s assumption is defined. The specification and the assumption are no longer typographically indistinguishable.
